title: Ashtpadi 14, salok: give up cleverness
hook: taj siaanap: give up cleverness and remember the Lord (Sukhmani 14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 13, rasnaa, and your line: guard the tongue. How did a day without gossip go? It's the end of a week that went low and stayed there: lowest is highest, humility first, honor the good, slander harms the slanderer, bless instead, guard the tongue. Today, the fourteenth ashtpadi. Day four hundred ninety.

You're in the shower, rehearsing. If I say this to my boss, then she'll say that, and then I'll mention the other thing, and that way it looks like it was her idea. Version two. Version three. The water runs, the plan gets cleverer and cleverer, and somewhere around version five you notice that you're not actually solving anything. You're just circling. The fourteenth ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens with a two-word instruction for exactly that state: taj siaanap. Today: give up the cleverness.
screen: `IN THE SHOWER, REHEARSING.` → `VERSION TWO. VERSION FIVE.` → `TAJ SIAANAP.`

segments.voice: Here's the salok, in paraphrase. Give up your cleverness, good people, and remember the Lord, the King. Keep in your mind hope in the One alone. Then, Nanak, pain, doubt and fear depart. Taj: give up, let go, abandon. Siaanap: cleverness. It comes from siaanaa, a Punjabi word that can mean wise, but also shrewd, crafty, the one who always has an angle. And that second sense is the one the salok means. Be careful here, because this is easy to misread. Sukhmani isn't against thinking. Guru Nanak praised the person who reflects on learning, and Sikh history is full of scholars, poets and builders. Siaanap is something narrower: the scheming mind, the one that's always calculating how to come out on top, how to arrange people, how to secure every outcome in advance. Why let that go? Look at what the salok promises in its place. Three things depart: dookh, pain; bharam, doubt; and bhau, fear. That's a precise list, and it's the list of what the scheming mind produces. The shower plan isn't really about the boss. It's fear, wearing a clever coat. The more angles you calculate, the more angles there are to be afraid of. The salok's alternative is simple to say and hard to do: one hope, kept in the mind, ek aas. Not a dozen backup plans, each with its own worry attached. One place to rest. Tomorrow and the next day the ashtpadi will turn to where that hope should and shouldn't rest. Today, only the first move: put the clever plan down.
screen: `TAJ: LET GO. SIAANAP: CLEVERNESS.` · `NOT THINKING, BUT SCHEMING.` · `PAIN, DOUBT AND FEAR DEPART.` · `EK AAS: ONE HOPE.` · then, large: `DROP THE CLEVERNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one scheme. Bring to mind a plan you've been circling, a conversation you keep rehearsing, an outcome you're trying to arrange. Hold it for a moment and see it clearly, all its versions. Then, on an out-breath, set it down. You can still act tomorrow; you're only putting down the circling. Rest in one simple hope instead of ten clever angles. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on the out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Siaanap, cleverness, shrewdness. The salok says: give it up, keep one hope, and pain, doubt and fear depart.
Your line: drop the cleverness. Today, when you catch yourself rehearsing an angle, stop and ask: what's the plain, straight version of this? Day four hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib open the fourteenth ashtpadi with the salok beginning taj siaanap, give up cleverness, and many read it as a turn from scheming toward a single hope in God.

myth: Sukhmani's fourteenth salok tells people to stop thinking
siaanap is scheming cleverness; Sikh tradition prizes reflection and learning.
the salok promises that pain, doubt and fear depart
dookh, bharam and bhau: the same things the scheming mind produces.
the salok recommends keeping many hopes as backup
ek aas: keep hope in the One alone.

fork.setup: you're in the shower, on version five of a plan to outmaneuver someone. what does the fourteenth salok say?
options: give up the cleverness and keep one hope.
fork.reveal: taj siaanap: drop the cleverness. the salok says that, with hope in the One, pain, doubt and fear depart.

original.note: Gurmukhi: siaanap, cleverness, shrewdness, from siaanaa, clever or wise.

trapdoor: what you thought: give up cleverness means don't be smart.
what it means: put down the scheming, angle-calculating mind and rest in one hope.
what a scholar hears: siaanaa covers both wise and crafty in Punjabi; the salok pairs giving it up with ek aas, one hope, and names three results, dookh, bharam, bhau.

notes: Salok of ashtpadi 14 paraphrased: taj-hu siaanap sur janahu simrahu har har raai; ek aas har man rakhahu Nanak dookh bharam bhau jaai. Confirm Ang 281 and the gloss of sur janahu as 'good people'.
Guru Nanak's line vidiaa veechaaree taan parupkaaree placed at Ang 356: confirm.
Gurmukhi spelling ਸਿਆਨਪ as it appears in this salok: confirm.
